trial_name: SAFE — Albumin vs Saline for Fluid Resuscitation in ICU (2004)
citation: SAFE Study Investigators. A Comparison of Albumin and Saline for Fluid Resuscitation in the Intensive Care Unit. N Engl J Med. 2004;350:2247–2256
one_liner: In a broad adult ICU population, 4% albumin vs 0.9% saline for resuscitation resulted in no difference in 28-day mortality (20.9% vs 21.1%; RR 0.99; 95% CI 0.91–1.09).

pico.population: Adult ICU patients requiring intravascular volume resuscitation; mean APACHE II ~19; excluded post-cardiac surgery, liver transplant, burns
pico.intervention: 4% human albumin (Albumex) for all ICU resuscitation up to day 28

background.existing_knowledge: Intravenous fluid resuscitation is near-universal in ICU; small treatment effects could translate to large population impact. Physiological arguments for colloids (oncotic pressure, less volume) competed with concerns about endothelial leak. A 1998 systematic review reported higher mortality with albumin, creating uncertainty.
background.knowledge_gap: Existing evidence was dominated by small, heterogeneous studies and meta-analyses; a large, blinded RCT was needed to resolve the 'albumin safety' question in contemporary ICU care.
background.hypothesis: Clinically meaningful differences in mortality were possible, but direction was uncertain given conflicting prior evidence.

methods.setting: 16 ICUs in Australia and New Zealand; fluid use only during ICU stay, not pre-ICU.

inclusion: Adults admitted to ICU where treating clinician determined intravascular volume resuscitation was required
exclusion: ICU admission after cardiac surgery, liver transplantation, or burns

methods.intervention: 4% human albumin solution (Albumex, CSL) used for all episodes of fluid resuscitation in ICU until ICU discharge/death or day 28. Dose/rate at clinician discretion. Masked 500 mL bottles and administration sets.
methods.comparison: 0.9% saline (normal saline) used for all episodes of fluid resuscitation in ICU until ICU discharge/death or day 28. Maintenance fluids, nutrition, and blood products permitted at clinician discretion in both groups.
methods.blinding: Double-blind (participants, clinicians, trial staff, outcome assessors). Masking cartons, identical bottles, and dedicated administration sets; blinding effectiveness formally assessed before trial.
methods.sample_size_power: 7000 patients planned to detect a 3% absolute difference in 28-day mortality (from ~15% to ~12%) with 90% power at two-sided α=0.05.
methods.follow_up: 28 days after randomisation; daily ICU data for first 7 days, then every 3rd day to day 28 or ICU discharge.

headline_bullets: 28-day mortality was identical: 20.9% albumin vs 21.1% saline (RR 0.99; 95% CI 0.91–1.09; P=0.87).
No benefit in secondary outcomes: organ failure, length of stay, ventilation, or RRT days.

Predefined subgroups: non-significant trend toward benefit in severe sepsis (RR 0.87; P=0.09) but signal of harm in trauma (RR 1.36; P=0.06), driven entirely by traumatic brain injury (RR 1.62; P=0.009).

outcomes_table.note: Vital status known for 6933 patients (67 missing). Survival curves similar (log-rank P=0.96).

outcomes_table.outcome: ICU length of stay (days), mean ± SD
Hospital length of stay (days), mean ± SD
Duration of mechanical ventilation (days), mean ± SD
Duration of renal-replacement therapy (days), mean ± SD

outcomes_table.note: Full distribution; data available for 2649 (albumin) and 2673 (saline). No significant difference.

subgroup_table.note: Excess 21 deaths in albumin group; P=0.009 for this analysis.

safety: No significant difference in new organ failure (SOFA-based) between groups (P=0.85).
Post-hoc analysis in traumatic brain injury: higher 28-day mortality with albumin (RR 1.62, P=0.009), an important safety signal.
No other safety concerns identified; adverse events not formally reported beyond organ failure distribution.

domains.notes: Central web-based minimisation stratified by ICU and trauma status; concealed using identical masked bottles/sets.
Double-blind; objective primary outcome (mortality) limits bias; secondary outcomes relatively objective and stratified by site.
Vital status missing for 67/7000 (1.0%): 26 albumin vs 41 saline; 56 due to withdrawn consent. Study fluid not given to 197 (2.8%), balanced between groups.

Resuscitation with non-study fluid: 309 albumin (8.8%) vs 375 saline (10.7%); clinician preference in 68 vs 103. Physiologic separation achieved: lower study fluid volumes (day 1: 1184 vs 1565 mL, P<0.001), lower net positive balance (day 1: 1544 vs 1991 mL, P<0.001), higher serum albumin (day 2: 30.8 vs 24.5 g/L, P<0.001).

Groups balanced for age, APACHE II (18.7 vs 19.0), mechanical ventilation (63.8% vs 64.8%), and baseline albumin (27.4 vs 27.7 g/L). Small imbalance in baseline CVP (9.0 vs 8.6 mm Hg, P=0.03) with unclear relevance.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is strong for the primary outcome due to concealed central randomisation, effective blinding, objective endpoint, and minimal missing outcome data; interpretability is more limited for subgroup signals due to multiplicity and lower power.

domains.notes: Broad adult ICU case-mix in closed multidisciplinary ICUs; APACHE II ~19 suggesting moderate-to-severe illness. Included trauma (~17%), severe sepsis (~18%), small ARDS (~2%). Excluded burns, post-cardiac surgery, post-liver transplant, paediatrics.

Findings generalise best to adult ICU resuscitation in comparable high-income settings. Only 4% albumin tested; results do not directly apply to 20–25% albumin or balanced crystalloids. Fluids outside ICU were not controlled, limiting translation to ED/pre-hospital or perioperative pathways.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is high for adult ICU resuscitation in similar settings, but limited for excluded populations (burns, cardiac surgery/transplant, paediatrics) and for other albumin concentrations or crystalloid formulations.

strengths: Large sample size (n=7000) with precise estimation of average treatment effect.
Double-blind design with robust masking and objective primary outcome.
Pragmatic protocol embedded in routine ICU practice, enhancing applicability.
Clear separation in physiological markers (serum albumin, CVP) and administered volume/net balance, supporting mechanistic plausibility.
limitations: Not powered to detect modest but clinically relevant subgroup effects; multiple comparisons increase false-positive risk.
Only 4% albumin tested; hyperoncotic albumin or albumin-targeting strategies not addressed.
Resuscitation fluids outside ICU not controlled.
Follow-up limited to 28 days; longer-term functional outcomes (especially for brain injury) not assessed.

critical_appraisal.summary: High-quality pragmatic RCT with robust methodology and precise estimate of no mortality difference between 4% albumin and saline; subgroup signals (sepsis benefit, traumatic brain injury harm) are hypothesis-generating due to multiplicity and lack of power.
strengths: Large, blinded, concealed allocation; objective primary outcome; pragmatic design.
weaknesses: Subgroup analyses underpowered and at risk of false positives; limited to 4% albumin; no long-term functional outcomes; no cost analysis.

sections.authors_conclusion: In a heterogeneous adult ICU population, 4% albumin and 0.9% saline produced clinically equivalent 28-day mortality (RR 0.99; 95% CI 0.91 to 1.09). This supports crystalloids as an acceptable default resuscitation fluid when albumin is being considered primarily for volume expansion.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Albumin is not superior to saline for fluid resuscitation in general ICU patients; crystalloids remain first-line. Albumin should be avoided in traumatic brain injury.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients requiring volume resuscitation, excluding burns, post-cardiac surgery, and liver transplant recipients.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: This does not mean albumin is harmful in all contexts; it may still be considered in septic shock after large crystalloid volumes, though the sepsis signal was not confirmed in dedicated trials.
implementation_caveats: Avoid albumin in traumatic brain injury, even in the presence of hemodynamic instability.
Consider cost and availability; no proven superiority over crystalloids for most patients.

controversies.notes: A 1998 systematic review reported higher mortality with albumin, motivating the need for a definitive blinded RCT. SAFE directly addressed this uncertainty.
Critics argued that a heterogeneous population could obscure subgroup benefits (e.g., sepsis) or harms; the trial powered only for overall mortality, not subgroup-specific effects.

Some correspondence noted that CVP ~9 mm Hg might indicate less severe volume depletion than implied by 'resuscitation,' potentially reducing detectable benefit; authors countered that contemporary practice resuscitates early.
The 13% relative risk reduction in severe sepsis (RR 0.87, P=0.09) was controversial; subsequent ALBIOS trial found no overall mortality benefit with albumin in sepsis, tempering enthusiasm.
Post-hoc signal of increased mortality with albumin in TBI (RR 1.62, P=0.009) led to focused analyses and practice change. Later observational and trial data reinforced avoidance of albumin in TBI.
SAFE used 4% albumin vs 0.9% saline; questions remain about hyperoncotic albumin (20–25%) or balanced crystalloids as comparators, which have different acid-base and chloride load profiles.

Guidelines (e.g., Surviving Sepsis Campaign, Brain Trauma Foundation) now recommend crystalloids as first-line resuscitation and reserve albumin for selected contexts, while advising against albumin in traumatic brain injury.

context_related_trials.relation: Randomised trial of albumin replacement in severe sepsis/septic shock; found no overall mortality benefit, counterbalancing SAFE’s sepsis subgroup trend.
Colloids vs crystalloids in ICU; did not show 28-day mortality benefit but suggested potential longer-term differences, reinforcing that fluid class effects are time- and outcome-dependent.
Subsequent detailed analysis of the SAFE traumatic brain injury cohort confirmed higher mortality with albumin, shifting practice away from albumin in this population.

unresolved_questions: Does 4% albumin confer a mortality benefit in severe sepsis when targeted to specific hemodynamic or biomarker-guided protocols?
What are the long-term functional outcomes and quality of life after albumin vs saline resuscitation, particularly in neurologically injured patients?
Would hyperoncotic (20–25%) albumin or albumin combined with balanced crystalloids yield different results?
What is the cost-effectiveness of albumin in ICU settings, especially given its higher acquisition cost without proven survival benefit?

numbers_to_remember: n=7000 randomised; 28-day mortality: albumin 20.9% vs saline 21.1%
Traumatic brain injury subanalysis: RR 1.62; P=0.009 (excess 21 deaths)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Albumin is not better than saline for most ICU fluid resuscitation, but it may harm patients with traumatic brain injury.
